title: Association Between β-Adrenoreceptor Agonists and Antagonists and Parkinson's Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Szmigiel A, da Rocha MM, Browne K, Morales D, Olsen DB, Warren-Gash C, et al.
population: 22 observational and intervention studies to December 2024 reporting relative risks of Parkinson's disease with beta-adrenoceptor agonists or antagonists
funder: No specific funding was received for this study. Two authors are funded by Wellcome fellowships (220283/Z/20/Z and 225868/Z/22/Z); one author holds grants from NIHR, GSK and AIR@InnoHK.
authorConflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
result: Twenty of 22 studies had a high risk of bias in at least one domain; control for smoking, a protective factor for Parkinson's disease, was deficient or lacking in 12. Summary relative risk for beta2-agonists 0.93 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.03; 11 studies) and for salbutamol 0.88 (0.77 to 1.01; 7 studies); short-acting beta2-agonists 0.91 (0.88 to 0.95; 6 studies), long-acting 0.85 (0.76 to 0.96; 5 studies). Restricting to higher-quality subgroups weakened the associations or removed their significance. The funnel plot for beta2-agonists suggested publication bias (Egger p = 0.03). The authors conclude that the evidence does not support a causal association and that significant associations are most likely explained by protopathic bias and confounding; a 2018 EMA PRAC signal procedure found insufficient evidence to update product information.
